text:
Recent work supports multi-scale interest modeling, but learned change-point boundaries are less established in the retrieved sources. [ScaleRec (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306457325002596) partitions histories into patches at multiple lengths, combines local Gaussian-kernel cross-attention with inter-patch self-attention, and adaptively filters redundant signals. Its segmentation uses multiple granularities rather than demonstrated learned intent boundaries. [ICSRec (WSDM 2024)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3616855.3635773) constructs subsequences through dynamic sliding and learns intent representations using coarse/fine contrastive objectives; shared next-item targets provide weak intent supervision without metadata. [PoMRec (2025)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40266875/) incorporates both mean and variance into multi-interest representations, offering a way to distinguish concentrated interests from dispersed interactions.

A plausible lightweight adaptation—not a validated result—is a causal soft-boundary gate using adjacent embedding similarity and timestamp gaps, pooling several recent segments and routing between current-segment, recurring-interest, and global-history representations. Repeated interest could accumulate support across segments while isolated events receive less weight, without assuming recent events are always preferable. Segment pooling could reduce attention cost, although routing overhead needs measurement. [MGUI (2026)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11506283) provides related precedent through time-aware gating, group-level capsule modeling, and user-specific expert fusion. For this benchmark, compare learned segmentation against fixed multi-scale windows and the five-item residual using macro validation HR@10; measure sensitivity to history truncation, older-event removal, and repeated-interest frequency before attributing gains to intent boundaries or recency.
